summary: Title slide introducing an introductory programming assignment presented by Sam Lee.
questions: What is the assignment about, and what will you cover in the next few slides?

summary: The slide states the assignment's task: read student names and scores from a CSV, sort them highest to lowest, and print the top 10 and class average.
claims: The program must read a CSV file of student names and scores.
Students must be sorted from highest to lowest score.
The program must print the top 10 students and the class average.
questions: Which sorting method did you choose, and why was it suitable for this task?
How does your program handle malformed rows in the CSV file?

summary: The slide claims the team wrote its own bubble sort and that it is as good as Python's built-in quicksort-based sorted().
claims: Bubble sort is the fastest sorting algorithm with O(n log n) complexity
The team's own bubble sort is just as good as sorted()
weak_points: Bubble sort is O(n^2) in the average and worst case, not O(n log n), and it is not the fastest general-purpose sorting algorithm; O(n log n) describes merge sort, quicksort and heapsort.
Python's sorted() uses Timsort, a hybrid merge sort, not quicksort, so the stated reason is factually wrong.
'Just as good' is asserted with no benchmark, dataset size, or timing comparison, and it conflicts with the complexity argument made on the same slide.
questions: Why do you say bubble sort is O(n log n) when its average case is O(n squared)?
What does sorted() actually use in CPython, and how did you measure that your sort is just as good?
Did you time your bubble sort against sorted() on the same data?

summary: Shows Python code that loads student name-score rows from a CSV, bubble-sorts them by score descending, then prints the top 10 and the class average.
claims: The program loads student names and scores from grades.csv and sorts them from highest to lowest score using bubble sort.
The program prints the top 10 students and the class average score.
weak_points: The slide is too dense to present, with about 19 lines of code in small monospace text; the audience cannot follow it in the time available, so ask which few lines matter most.

The load function assumes every CSV row has exactly two fields and that scores are integers, with no handling for a header row, blank lines or malformed values, and the code does not check these assumptions.
Bubble sort is O(n^2) in the worst and average case, which conflicts with the previous slide's claim that it is the fastest sorting algorithm with O(n log n) complexity.
questions: Which three lines of this code are most important for the audience to understand?
What happens if grades.csv has a header row or a non-integer score?
Why use bubble sort instead of Python's built-in sorted(), given the slide 3 claim?
Does the average divide by zero if the file is empty?

summary: The slide claims the team's sorting program is 5x faster, sorting 500 students in 0.2 seconds, shown with an unlabeled two-bar chart.
claims: The program is 5x faster than the comparison.
weak_points: The 5x speedup has no stated baseline: the comparison method, its runtime, and the hardware are not given.
The bar chart has no axis labels, units, or legend, so the audience cannot tell what the bars measure.
The deck says bubble sort is O(n log n), which is false: bubble sort is O(n^2), and Python's sorted() uses Timsort rather than quicksort, so the 5x result conflicts with the stated approach.
questions: What exactly is the 5x compared against, and what were the baseline runtimes?
What do the two bars measure, and what are their units?
Is 0.2 seconds for 500 students representative, and how was it timed?

summary: The slide concludes that the program was tested on three CSV files, is bug-free, and is ready for any school to use.
claims: Tested on 3 CSV files: all worked
Ready for any school to use
weak_points: Three test files cannot establish that the program is bug-free; no test coverage, edge cases, or failure inputs are reported.
The claim of readiness for any school generalises far beyond three test files, with no evidence about different CSV formats, class sizes, or data quality.
questions: What do the three CSV files contain, and what edge cases did you test?
What specifically would have to be true before a school other than ours could safely use this?
